The flu (influenza) is a viral infection that comes on quickly and can make you feel very sick. Common signs that you have the flu include:

• Fever – a high temperature, often 100°F (38°C) or higher, that may come on suddenly  
• Chills – feeling cold and shivering even though you have a fever  
• Headache – a throbbing or pressure feeling in the head  
• Muscle aches – soreness in the arms, legs, or back, sometimes so strong it feels like a “body ache”  
• Fatigue – feeling extremely tired and having little energy, even after resting  
• Cough – usually a dry, hacking cough that can become more severe over a few days  
• Sore throat – a scratchy or painful feeling in the throat, making swallowing uncomfortable  
• Runny or stuffy nose – nasal discharge or congestion that can make breathing through the nose difficult  
• Sometimes nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea – more common in children than adults  

These symptoms often appear all at once and can last about a week, though feeling weak may continue for a bit longer. If you notice very high fever, trouble breathing, chest pain, sudden dizziness, or confusion, seek medical help right away, as these can be signs of a more serious illness.

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly, so the signs can be mild at first. Common symptoms include:

• Feeling very thirsty more often than usual – the body tries to replace fluid lost through extra urination.  
• Going to the bathroom a lot, especially at night – this is called polyuria, which means frequent urination.  
• Feeling unusually hungry even after eating – the body isn’t using sugar properly, so it signals for more food.  
• Unexplained weight loss – despite eating more, the body may break down fat and muscle for energy.  
• Feeling very tired or low on energy – cells aren’t getting enough usable sugar.  
• Blurred vision – high blood sugar can cause the eye’s lens to swell, making things look fuzzy.  
• Slow healing of cuts, bruises, or infections – high sugar levels can affect the body’s ability to repair tissue.  
• Numbness, tingling, or pain in the hands or feet – this is called peripheral neuropathy, a nerve problem that can start early.  

Sometimes people with type 2 diabetes have no noticeable symptoms at all, which is why regular screening is important, especially if you have risk factors such as being overweight, having a family history of diabetes, or being over age 45. If you notice any of these signs, talk to a health professional for testing and advice.

High blood pressure (also called hypertension) often does not cause any obvious feeling, which is why many people call it a “silent” condition. However, when symptoms do appear, they can include:

• Headaches, especially at the back of the head or in the morning  
• Dizziness or feeling light‑headed  
• Blurred or double vision  
• Shortness of breath, even with mild activity  
• Chest discomfort or a feeling of pressure in the chest  
• Fatigue or feeling unusually tired  
• Nosebleeds that happen more often than usual  
• Blood in the urine or a change in how often you need to go to the bathroom  

Because most people with high blood pressure feel fine, the best way to know if you have it is to have your blood pressure measured regularly by a doctor, pharmacist, or with a home monitor. If you notice any of the symptoms above, especially if they come on suddenly or are severe, you should contact a health professional right away.

Iron deficiency anemia happens when your body doesn’t have enough iron to make healthy red blood cells. Without enough iron, you may notice several signs and symptoms. They can develop slowly, so it’s a good idea to pay attention if you notice a few of them together.

• Feeling unusually tired or weak – your body isn’t getting enough oxygen, so you get low energy.  
• Shortness of breath, especially during activities that used to be easy, like climbing stairs.  
• Pale skin, especially on the face, inside the lower eyelids, or on the nail beds.  
• Fast or irregular heartbeat – the heart works harder to move the limited oxygen around.  
• Cold hands and feet – reduced blood flow can make extremities feel chilly.  
• Headaches or dizziness – low oxygen to the brain can cause these sensations.  
• Cravings for non‑food items such as ice, dirt, or starch (a condition called pica).  
• Brittle or spoon‑shaped nails, or nails that break easily.  
• Restless legs syndrome – an uncomfortable urge to move the legs, often at night.  
• Poor concentration or difficulty thinking clearly.  

If you notice several of these symptoms, especially if they last for weeks or get worse, it’s a good idea to see a health professional. A simple blood test can confirm whether iron deficiency anemia is the cause and guide appropriate treatment.

Asthma is a condition that makes the airways in the lungs become narrow and inflamed. When this happens, people notice several common signs:

• Shortness of breath – feeling like you can’t get enough air, especially during activity or at night.  
• Wheezing – a high‑pitched whistling sound when you breathe out.  
• Coughing – often dry (no mucus) and may be worse at night, early in the morning, or after exercise.  
• Chest tightness – a feeling that something is squeezing or pressing on the chest.

These symptoms can come and go. Sometimes they are mild and only appear with triggers such as pollen, cold air, smoke, or strong emotions. At other times they can become more intense, leading to an asthma attack, which may include rapid breathing, severe wheezing, and difficulty speaking. If you notice any of these signs, especially if they happen repeatedly, it’s a good idea to talk to a healthcare professional.

Gastro‑esophageal reflux disease, or GERD, happens when stomach acid flows back up into the tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach (the esophagus). This back‑flow can irritate the lining of the esophagus and cause a range of signs that many people notice.

Common symptoms of GERD include:

• Heartburn – a burning feeling behind the breastbone that often gets worse after eating or when lying down.  
• Regurgitation – a sour or bitter taste in the mouth caused by stomach contents coming back up.  
• Chest discomfort – pressure, tightness, or pain in the chest that can be mistaken for a heart problem.  
• Difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) – feeling that food gets stuck or moves slowly down the throat.  
• Chronic cough – a persistent cough that isn’t caused by a cold or asthma.  
• Hoarseness or sore throat – irritation from acid reaching the throat and voice box.  
• Feeling of a lump in the throat (globus sensation) – a sensation that something is stuck even when nothing is there.  
• Bloating or excessive burping – frequent belching or a feeling of fullness after meals.  
• Nausea or vomiting – especially after large or fatty meals.  

If any of these signs appear often, especially after meals or when lying down, it’s a good idea to talk with a healthcare professional. Early treatment can help control symptoms and prevent damage to the esophagus.

Strep throat is an infection of the throat caused by a type of bacteria called group A streptococcus. It can feel similar to a regular sore throat, but there are some clues that point to strep. Common symptoms include:

• Sudden, severe sore throat that makes swallowing painful  
• Red and swollen tonsils, sometimes with white or yellow patches (pus) on them  
• Fever of 101 °F (38.5 °C) or higher  
• Swollen, tender lymph nodes on the sides of the neck  
• Headache  
• Nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain, especially in children  
• A feeling of general tiredness or being unwell (fatigue)  
• Sometimes a rash that looks like tiny red spots (called scarlet fever)  

Symptoms that are **less** typical for strep throat and more common with a viral cold include a runny nose, cough, hoarseness, and watery eyes. If you have several of the signs above—especially a sore throat that started quickly, fever, and white spots on the tonsils—it’s a good idea to see a health professional. They can do a quick throat swab test and, if it is strep, prescribe antibiotics to help you get better faster and prevent complications.

Hepatitis C is an infection of the liver caused by a virus.  In many people the infection does not cause any noticeable problems at first, so they may feel completely normal for months or even years.  When symptoms do appear, they can be mild at first and may be easy to miss.  

Typical signs and symptoms include:

• Feeling unusually tired or weak – a general lack of energy that does not go away with rest.  
• Loss of appetite or feeling full quickly, which can lead to unintentional weight loss.  
• Nausea or occasional vomiting.  
• Abdominal discomfort, especially a dull ache in the upper right side where the liver sits.  
• Dark‑colored urine, which looks amber or brown, caused by extra bilirubin (a pigment the liver normally clears).  
• Pale‑colored stool, which can be lighter than normal because of reduced bile flow.  
• Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes (jaundice) – a yellow tint that appears when the liver cannot process bilirubin fast enough.  
• Fever, chills, or muscle and joint aches, similar to a mild flu.  

Because many people with hepatitis C have no symptoms, the infection is often discovered through blood tests done for other reasons or during routine screening. If you think you might have been exposed to the virus, or if you notice any of the above signs, talk to a health professional about getting tested. Early diagnosis makes treatment much more effective.

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed by measuring how much sugar (glucose) is in the blood. Doctors use a few different tests, and each one has a specific number that tells them whether diabetes is present.

**Common tests**

• **Fasting plasma glucose (FPG)** – You fast (no food or drink except water) for at least 8 hours, then a blood sample is taken.  
 – A level of 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher on two separate occasions means diabetes.  
 – Levels between 100 mg/dL and 125 mg/dL are called “prediabetes,” a warning sign that diabetes could develop.

• **Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)** – After the same overnight fast, you drink a sugary liquid containing 75 grams of glucose. Blood is drawn again after 2 hours.  
 – A 2‑hour level of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher on two separate tests indicates diabetes.  
 – Levels from 140 mg/dL to 199 mg/dL are considered prediabetes.

• **Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) test** – This blood test measures the average blood‑sugar level over the past 2‑3 months. It looks at how much sugar is attached to the protein hemoglobin inside red blood cells.  
 – An A1c of 6.5 % or higher on two separate occasions confirms diabetes.  
 – An A1c between 5.7 % and 6.4 % is the range for prediabetes.

• **Random plasma glucose** – A single blood sample is taken at any time, without fasting. If the level is 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher **and** you have classic diabetes symptoms (such as increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, or blurry vision), diabetes can be diagnosed right away.

**Who should be screened?**

• Adults age 45 and older, even if they feel well.  
• Younger adults who have risk factors such as obesity, a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol, or a history of gestational diabetes (diabetes during pregnancy).  
• People from ethnic groups with higher diabetes rates (for example, African‑American, Hispanic, Native American, Asian‑American, or Pacific Islander).

If any of the test results are in the diabetic range, the doctor will usually repeat the test on a different day to be sure. Once diabetes is confirmed, further evaluation is done to check for complications and to start a treatment plan that may include lifestyle changes, medication, and regular monitoring.

High blood pressure, also called hypertension, is diagnosed by measuring the pressure of blood flowing through your arteries. The process is simple but must be done carefully to be accurate.

First, a health professional uses a cuff that inflates around your upper arm. The cuff squeezes the arm and then slowly releases, while a device listens to the pulse or reads the pressure electronically. The result is written as two numbers, for example 120/80 mm Hg.  

• The first (higher) number is the **systolic** pressure – the force when the heart beats and pushes blood out.  
• The second (lower) number is the **diastolic** pressure – the force when the heart rests between beats.

To decide whether you have high blood pressure, doctors follow these steps:

1. **Take several readings on different days** – One single measurement can be affected by stress, caffeine, or a full bladder. Usually three or more readings taken at least a week apart are needed.  
2. **Use the correct cuff size and position** – The cuff must fit snugly around the arm and be placed at heart level.  
3. **Follow standard thresholds** – In most guidelines, blood pressure is considered high if:  
   • Systolic is 130 mm Hg or higher, or  
   • Diastolic is 80 mm Hg or higher.  
   (Values below these limits are usually called normal or elevated, depending on how close they are.)  
4. **Confirm with additional tests if needed** – If the office readings are high, a doctor may ask you to:  
   • Keep a home blood‑pressure log, measuring yourself twice each morning and evening for a week.  
   • Wear a portable monitor for 24 hours (ambulatory blood‑pressure monitoring) to see how pressure changes throughout the day and night.  

If the repeated measurements stay at or above the threshold, the diagnosis of hypertension is made. The doctor will then look for possible causes (like kidney problems or certain medicines) and discuss lifestyle changes or medication to bring the pressure down.

Pneumonia is usually diagnosed by a combination of talking with you, listening to your lungs, and doing a few simple tests.

**1. Talk about your symptoms**  
• The doctor will ask when your cough started, if you have fever, shortness of breath, chest pain, or a feeling of tiredness.  
• They may also ask about recent illnesses, travel, exposure to sick people, or any chronic health problems you have.

**2. Physical exam**  
• The doctor listens to your chest with a stethoscope. A “crackling” or “rattling” sound (called crackles) can suggest fluid in the lungs, which is common in pneumonia.  
• They also check your breathing rate, heart rate, and temperature.

**3. Chest X‑ray**  
• This is a quick picture of the inside of your chest. It shows areas where the lungs look denser or cloudy, which is a typical sign of pneumonia.  
• If the X‑ray is unclear, a CT scan (a more detailed picture) may be ordered.

**4. Pulse oximetry**  
• A small sensor is placed on your finger to measure how much oxygen is in your blood. Low oxygen levels can indicate that pneumonia is affecting breathing.

**5. Laboratory tests**  
• **Blood test** – looks for signs of infection such as an increased white‑blood‑cell count.  
• **Sputum test** – you cough up a sample of mucus (sputum) that is sent to the lab to see which germs (bacteria, viruses, or fungi) are causing the infection.  
• **Urine test** – in some cases, a urine sample can help identify certain bacteria that cause pneumonia.

**6. Additional tests for special situations**  
• **Bronchoscopy** – a thin tube with a light is passed into the airway to collect deeper samples; used when the cause is unclear or the patient is very sick.  
• **Chest ultrasound** – can be used, especially in children or in the intensive‑care setting, to look for fluid or infection.

**Putting it together**  
The doctor combines the information from your symptoms, the lung sounds, the X‑ray, and any lab results to decide whether you have pneumonia and what type of germ is likely causing it. This helps choose the right treatment, such as antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia or other medicines for viral causes.

Anemia is found when a doctor looks at your symptoms, does a physical exam, and runs a few simple lab tests. The main steps are:

• **Medical history and symptoms** – You’ll be asked about tiredness, shortness of breath, pale skin, fast heartbeat, or any bleeding you’ve had. The doctor also checks for diet, medications, family history and any chronic illnesses.

• **Physical exam** – The doctor looks for signs such as pale skin, a rapid pulse, or an enlarged spleen or liver. They may also listen to your heart and lungs.

• **Blood test (complete blood count, or CBC)** – This is the key test. It measures:
  – Hemoglobin: the protein that carries oxygen. Low levels mean anemia.
  – Hematocrit: the percentage of blood that is made up of red blood cells. Low values also indicate anemia.
  – Red‑cell count and size (mean corpuscular volume, MCV). The size helps tell what type of anemia it might be.
  – Reticulocyte count: how many new red blood cells the bone marrow is making. A high count suggests the body is trying to replace lost cells; a low count suggests the marrow isn’t making enough.

• **Additional blood tests to find the cause** – Depending on the CBC results, the doctor may order:
  – Iron studies (serum iron, ferritin, total iron‑binding capacity) to see if iron deficiency is the problem.
  – Vitamin B12 and folate levels, because low amounts can cause a different kind of anemia.
  – Tests for kidney function, because kidneys help make a hormone that stimulates red‑cell production.
  – Tests for inflammation or chronic disease, such as C‑reactive protein or erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

• **Other investigations if needed** – If the blood tests suggest blood loss or a specific disease, the doctor may do:
  – Stool test for hidden blood (occult blood test) to look for gastrointestinal bleeding.
  – Endoscopy or colonoscopy to view the digestive tract.
  – Bone‑marrow biopsy if a problem with blood‑cell production is suspected.

When the hemoglobin level is below the normal range for your age and sex (usually less than about 13 g/dL for men and 12 g/dL for women), and the other test results support it, the doctor confirms the diagnosis of anemia and then works to find the underlying cause.

Hypothyroidism is diagnosed by combining what a person feels, what a doctor finds on exam, and a few simple blood tests.

**1. Review of symptoms and medical history**  
A doctor will ask about common signs of an under‑active thyroid, such as feeling unusually tired, gaining weight, feeling cold, having dry skin or hair, constipation, or a slow heartbeat. They will also check for any family history of thyroid problems or other autoimmune diseases.

**2. Physical examination**  
During the exam the doctor may feel the neck to see if the thyroid gland feels enlarged or irregular. They will also listen to the heart, check reflexes, and look for other clues like puffiness around the eyes or swelling of the hands and feet.

**3. Blood tests**  
The most important step is measuring hormones in the blood:

• **TSH (thyroid‑stimulating hormone)** – This is the hormone the pituitary gland makes to tell the thyroid to work. In hypothyroidism the pituitary makes more TSH, so the level is usually high.  
• **Free T4 (free thyroxine)** – This is the main hormone the thyroid releases. In hypothyroidism the amount of free T4 is low.  
• **Free T3 (free triiodothyronine)** – Sometimes measured if the doctor suspects a specific type of thyroid problem.  
• **Thyroid antibodies** – Tests for antibodies such as anti‑TPO or anti‑thyroglobulin can show whether the immune system is attacking the thyroid, which is the most common cause (called Hashimoto’s thyroiditis).

**4. Additional tests when needed**  
If the blood results are unclear or if there is a suspicion of a nodule or other structural issue, the doctor may order:

• **Ultrasound of the neck** – Uses sound waves to look at the size and texture of the thyroid.  
• **Radioactive iodine uptake test** – Measures how well the thyroid takes up iodine, helping to differentiate types of thyroid disease.

**5. Screening in certain groups**  
Because hypothyroidism can develop slowly, doctors often check thyroid function in:

• Women over age 60  
• Pregnant women (early testing is important for the baby’s development)  
• People with a family history of thyroid disease  
• Individuals with other autoimmune conditions such as type 1 diabetes or celiac disease

If the TSH is high and the free T4 is low, the diagnosis of hypothyroidism is usually confirmed. The doctor will then discuss treatment options, typically a daily dose of synthetic thyroid hormone to bring the hormone levels back to normal.

Hepatitis B is diagnosed by a combination of questions, a quick physical check, and a few laboratory tests. The goal is to find evidence that the virus is present, see how the liver is doing, and decide whether the infection is new or has been around for a while.

**1. Medical history and physical exam**  
A doctor will ask about possible exposures (such as unprotected sex, sharing needles, or contact with infected blood) and look for signs of liver trouble, such as yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), abdominal pain, or swelling.

**2. Blood tests**  
The most important part of the diagnosis is a set of blood tests that look for specific proteins and genetic material from the virus.

• **HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen)** – This protein is part of the virus’s outer shell. If it is found in the blood, it means the person is currently infected.  
• **Anti‑HBs (antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen)** – This antibody shows up after the infection has cleared or after vaccination. It tells the doctor the person is protected.  
• **Anti‑HBc (antibody to hepatitis B core antigen)** – This antibody appears when the immune system has responded to the inner part of the virus. It can be of two types: IgM (appears early in a new infection) and IgG (stays long‑term).  
• **HBV DNA** – This test measures the amount of viral genetic material (the virus’s “blueprint”) in the blood. A higher number means the virus is actively replicating.  
• **Liver function tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin, etc.)** – These chemicals tell how well the liver is working and whether it is being damaged.

**3. Imaging studies**  
If the doctor wants to see the liver’s shape or look for complications, an ultrasound (sound‑wave picture) of the abdomen is often used. It is painless and shows whether the liver is enlarged, scarred, or has other problems.

**4. Liver biopsy (in selected cases)**  
Sometimes a tiny piece of liver tissue is taken with a thin needle to look under a microscope. This helps assess the amount of scarring (cirrhosis) when the other tests are unclear. It is not needed for most people.

**5. Special screening situations**  
• **Pregnant women** – All pregnant people are routinely tested for HBsAg so that newborns can receive preventive medicine right after birth.  
• **Newborns of infected mothers** – The baby receives hepatitis B vaccine and a dose of hepatitis B immune globulin within 12 hours of birth, then follow‑up testing to confirm they are not infected.  
• **People at high risk** – Those who use injection drugs, have multiple sexual partners, or live with someone who has hepatitis B are often screened regularly.

Putting the results together, the doctor can tell whether the infection is acute (new), chronic (lasting more than six months), or resolved, and can decide on the best plan for monitoring or treatment.

The flu (influenza) is a viral infection that usually gets better on its own, but treatment focuses on easing symptoms, staying hydrated, and preventing complications.

**Rest and fluids**  
• Get plenty of sleep and take it easy while your body fights the virus.  
• Drink water, clear soups, herbal tea, or electrolyte drinks to replace fluids lost from fever and sweating.  

**Medication for symptoms**  
• Over‑the‑counter pain relievers such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen can lower fever, relieve headache, and ease muscle aches.  
• Cough suppressants or expectorants can help with a dry cough or a cough that brings up mucus.  
• Decongestant tablets or nasal sprays can reduce a blocked nose, but they should not be used for more than a few days.

**Antiviral medicines**  
• Prescription antivirals (for example, oseltamivir) can shorten the illness by about a day if started within 48 hours of symptom onset.  
• These drugs are especially important for people at higher risk of serious flu complications, such as the elderly, young children, pregnant women, or those with chronic health conditions.

**When to see a health professional**  
• If you have difficulty breathing, chest pain, persistent high fever, severe vomiting, or confusion.  
• If symptoms suddenly get much worse after a brief improvement.  
• If you belong to a high‑risk group and the flu is not improving after a few days.

**Home care tips**  
• Keep the room at a comfortable temperature and use a humidifier to ease a dry throat.  
• Eat light, nutritious foods like fruits, vegetables, and broth to give your body energy.  
• Wash your hands frequently and avoid close contact with others to stop the virus from spreading.

Most healthy adults recover from the flu within one to two weeks. If you follow these steps and watch for warning signs, you can help your body heal and reduce the chance of complications.

Type 2 diabetes is managed with a combination of everyday habits, medicines and regular check‑ups. The goal is to keep blood‑sugar levels in a healthy range so the body works well and complications are avoided.

**Lifestyle changes**

• Eat a balanced diet – focus on vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins and healthy fats. Limit sugary drinks, sweets and large portions of refined carbs (like white bread).  
• Control portion sizes and spread meals throughout the day to avoid big spikes in blood sugar.  
• Be active – aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise (such as brisk walking, cycling or swimming) each week. Exercise helps the body use insulin more efficiently.  
• Lose excess weight if needed. Even a modest loss of 5‑10 % of body weight can improve blood‑sugar control.  
• Quit smoking and limit alcohol, both of which can worsen diabetes and heart health.

**Blood‑sugar monitoring**

• Check blood glucose at home using a finger‑stick meter or a continuous glucose monitor (a small sensor that measures sugar levels throughout the day).  
• Regular monitoring helps you see how food, activity and medicines affect your numbers and lets your doctor adjust treatment as needed.

**Medications**

If lifestyle changes alone are not enough, doctors add medicines that work in different ways:

• **Metformin** – the first‑line drug; it lowers the amount of sugar the liver releases and makes the body more sensitive to insulin.  
• **Sulfonylureas** – stimulate the pancreas to release more insulin.  
• **GLP‑1 receptor agonists** – mimic a natural hormone that increases insulin release after meals, slows digestion and can help with weight loss.  
• **SGLT2 inhibitors** – cause the kidneys to excrete extra sugar in the urine, also offering heart and kidney benefits.  
• **DPP‑4 inhibitors** – keep the body’s own insulin‑boosting hormones active longer.  
• **Insulin therapy** – sometimes needed if other medicines are not enough; short‑acting or long‑acting insulin is injected to replace or supplement the body’s own insulin.

Your doctor will choose the medication(s) based on your blood‑sugar levels, other health conditions, and how you respond to treatment.

**Regular medical follow‑up**

• Check blood‑sugar (A1C) every 3‑6 months. The A1C test shows average sugar levels over the past 2‑3 months.  
• Screen for complications such as eye problems, kidney disease, nerve damage and heart disease.  
• Update vaccinations (flu, pneumonia, COVID‑19) because diabetes can increase infection risk.

**When surgery is considered**

For some people with severe obesity, bariatric surgery (weight‑loss surgery) can dramatically improve blood‑sugar control and may even put diabetes into remission.

**Putting it all together**

Managing type 2 diabetes works best when you combine healthy eating, regular activity, monitoring, and the right medicines. Keep an open line of communication with your health‑care team, ask questions, and make adjustments as needed. Small, consistent steps can lead to big improvements in your health.

A urinary tract infection (UTI) is usually treated with medicines and simple home care. The goal is to clear the infection, relieve symptoms, and prevent it from coming back.

**Antibiotics**  
The main treatment is a short course of antibiotics, which are medicines that kill the bacteria causing the infection.  
• Your doctor will choose the specific antibiotic based on the type of bacteria and any recent antibiotic use.  
• Most people take the medicine for 3 to 7 days; a longer course may be needed for more serious infections.  
• It’s important to finish the whole prescription, even if you feel better before the pills are gone, to make sure all the bacteria are gone.

**Pain and symptom relief**  
While the antibiotics work, you can ease discomfort:  
• Over‑the‑counter pain relievers such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen can reduce pain and fever.  
• A medication called phenazopyridine (often sold as “Uristat” or similar) can calm burning or urgency while you wait for the antibiotics to take effect. It only treats symptoms, not the infection itself.

**Hydration**  
Drinking plenty of fluids helps flush bacteria out of the urinary system.  
• Aim for at least 8 glasses (about 2 liters) of water a day, unless your doctor tells you otherwise.  
• Cranberry juice or unsweetened cranberry products are sometimes suggested, but they are not a substitute for antibiotics.

**Follow‑up**  
• Most uncomplicated UTIs improve within a day or two. If symptoms persist after 2–3 days of antibiotics, or if they get worse at any time, contact your doctor.  
• For pregnant women, children, men, or people with kidney problems, doctors may order a urine test after treatment to be sure the infection is gone.

**Preventing future infections**  
After the infection clears, you can lower the chance of another UTI by:  
• Wiping from front to back after using the toilet (helps keep bacteria from the anus away from the urethra).  
• Urinating soon after sex, which helps wash out any bacteria that may have been pushed toward the bladder.  
• Drinking enough water each day to keep urine clear and frequent.  
• Avoiding irritating feminine products such as douches, powders, or strong soaps in the genital area.  

If you think you have a UTI, see a healthcare provider for a urine test and appropriate antibiotic prescription. Prompt treatment usually clears the infection quickly and prevents complications.

Asthma is a condition where the airways in the lungs become tight and inflamed, making it hard to breathe. Treatment focuses on two goals: stopping attacks quickly when they happen and keeping the lungs calm so attacks are less likely.

**Quick‑relief (rescue) medicines**  
These are used at the first sign of an asthma flare‑up to open the airways right away.

• Short‑acting bronchodilator inhaler – a puff that relaxes the muscles around the airway, letting air flow in more easily.  
• Nebulizer solution – a liquid form of the same medicine that can be breathed in through a mask, useful for young children or severe attacks.  

**Long‑term control medicines**  
These are taken every day to reduce the underlying inflammation and prevent attacks.

• Inhaled corticosteroid – a spray that goes into the lungs and lowers swelling; it’s the most common preventer medicine.  
• Long‑acting bronchodilator – a puff that keeps the airway muscles relaxed for many hours; it is usually combined with a corticosteroid in one inhaler.  
• Leukotriene modifier – a pill that blocks chemicals that cause airway tightening.  
• Biologic therapy – an injection for people with severe asthma that targets specific parts of the immune system; examples include medicines that block a protein called IgE or certain interleukins.  

**Other important parts of asthma care**

• **Trigger avoidance** – identify and stay away from things that set off symptoms, such as pollen, pet dander, smoke, strong odors, or cold air.  
• **Inhaler technique** – using the inhaler correctly ensures the medicine reaches the lungs; a healthcare provider can show the right steps.  
• **Monitoring** – using a peak‑flow meter or keeping a symptom diary helps you see how well the asthma is controlled.  
• **Written asthma action plan** – a simple chart that tells you what medicines to take at each level of symptoms and when to call a doctor or go to the emergency room.  

By combining quick‑relief inhalers for emergencies, daily control medicines to keep inflammation low, and lifestyle steps to avoid triggers, most people with asthma can lead active, normal lives. If symptoms are still frequent or severe, a doctor may adjust the medication dose or add newer treatments such as biologic injections. Regular follow‑up appointments are important to make sure the plan stays effective.

Gastro‑esophageal reflux disease (GERD) is when stomach acid frequently flows back into the tube that carries food to the stomach (the esophagus). The goal of treatment is to stop the reflux, heal any irritation, and prevent future problems.

**Lifestyle and diet changes**  
• Eat smaller meals and avoid large, heavy dinners.  
• Stay upright for at least two to three hours after eating; don’t lie down right away.  
• Raise the head of the bed about 6‑10 cm (a wedge pillow works too) to keep acid down while you sleep.  
• Avoid foods and drinks that relax the lower‑esophageal sphincter (the muscle that closes the opening between esophagus and stomach) or irritate the lining, such as:  
 – Spicy foods  
 – Citrus fruits and juices  
 – Tomato‑based sauces  
 – Chocolate  
 – Mint  
 – Caffeine and coffee  
 – Alcohol  
 – Carbonated drinks  
• Quit smoking; nicotine can weaken the muscle that keeps acid out of the esophagus.  
• Lose excess weight if you’re overweight; extra belly pressure can push acid upward.  
• Wear loose‑fitting clothing around the waist so it doesn’t squeeze the stomach.

**Medications**  
• Antacids (e.g., calcium carbonate) neutralize acid quickly and are useful for occasional heartburn.  
• H2‑blockers (e.g., ranitidine, famotidine) reduce the amount of acid the stomach makes; they work slower than antacids but last longer.  
• Proton‑pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as omeprazole, esomeprazole, or lansoprazole are the most powerful acid‑reducing drugs. They allow the esophagus to heal and are usually taken once daily before breakfast.  
• Prokinetic agents (e.g., metoclopramide) help the stomach empty faster, decreasing the chance of reflux; they are used less often because of side‑effects.

**When medication isn’t enough**  
If symptoms persist despite lifestyle changes and medicines, a doctor may suggest:

• Stronger or higher‑dose PPIs, sometimes taken twice a day.  
• Surgery or minimally invasive procedures to tighten the lower‑esophageal sphincter, such as:  
 – Laparoscopic fundoplication – the top part of the stomach is wrapped around the lower esophagus to reinforce the valve.  
 – Endoscopic techniques (e.g., radiofrequency treatment) that tighten the muscle without incisions.  

**Follow‑up care**  
• Regular check‑ups help ensure the lining of the esophagus is healing and that there are no complications like Barrett’s esophagus (a change in the lining that can increase cancer risk).  
• If you need to stay on PPIs for a long time, your doctor may monitor bone health, kidney function, and vitamin B12 levels, because prolonged acid suppression can affect these.

In most people, a combination of diet changes, weight control, and a short course of medication controls GERD effectively. Surgery is reserved for those whose symptoms remain severe despite these measures.

Iron deficiency anemia is treated by getting more iron into the body and fixing anything that is causing the loss of iron.

First, doctors usually give iron supplements. These are pills or liquids that contain iron that the body can absorb. Most people take them once a day for several months. It can take a few weeks to feel more energy, but the blood usually needs about three months of treatment to fill up the iron stores again.

Things that help the iron pills work better:

• Take the supplement on an empty stomach, or with a small amount of water or juice, unless it upsets your stomach.  
• Vitamin C (found in orange juice, strawberries, bell peppers) helps the body absorb iron, so having a source of vitamin C with the pill can be useful.  
• Avoid taking the iron pill at the same time as calcium‑rich foods, dairy, coffee, tea, or antacids, because these can block iron absorption.

If oral pills cause stomach upset or if the anemia is very severe, a doctor may give iron through a vein (intravenous iron). This puts iron directly into the bloodstream and works faster, but it is usually reserved for people who cannot tolerate pills or who need a quick fix.

Diet changes are also part of treatment. Eating foods that are naturally high in iron helps keep levels up after the supplements are finished. Good sources include:

• Red meat, poultry, and fish (these contain heme iron, which the body absorbs easily)  
• Beans, lentils, tofu, and fortified cereals (these have non‑heme iron, which is absorbed a bit less well)  
• Dark leafy greens like spinach and kale  
• Nuts and seeds  

Pairing these foods with vitamin C‑rich items (like citrus fruit, tomatoes, or bell peppers) improves absorption.

Sometimes iron loss is caused by another problem, such as:

• Heavy menstrual bleeding  
• Gastrointestinal bleeding from ulcers, hemorrhoids, or colon polyps  
• Certain medications or parasites  

Treating the underlying cause is essential. For example, if heavy periods are the issue, a doctor might prescribe hormonal therapy or other methods to reduce bleeding. If there is bleeding in the gut, the source may need to be fixed with medication, endoscopy, or surgery.

In very severe cases, when the blood count is dangerously low, a short‑term blood transfusion may be needed to quickly raise the number of red blood cells. This is usually a temporary measure while iron therapy takes effect.

Finally, doctors will check blood tests after a few weeks and then again after a few months to make sure the iron levels are rising and staying normal. The iron supplement is usually continued for a few months after the anemia is corrected to rebuild the body’s iron stores.

In summary, treatment includes:

• Oral iron pills (or IV iron if needed)  
• Vitamin C to help absorption  
• Iron‑rich foods and good eating habits  
• Fixing any source of ongoing blood loss  
• Monitoring blood tests to confirm recovery  

With these steps, most people recover fully and can prevent the anemia from coming back.

Eczema, also called atopic dermatitis, is a skin condition that makes the skin dry, itchy, and sometimes red or bumpy. Treatment focuses on three goals: keeping the skin moisturized, reducing inflammation, and avoiding things that make the rash worse.

**Moisturizing (skin barrier care)**
• Use a thick, fragrance‑free cream or ointment several times a day, especially after a bath.  
• Look for products that contain ingredients like ceramides, petrolatum, or glycerin, which help lock water into the skin.  
• Apply the moisturizer while the skin is still a little damp; this traps extra moisture.

**Bathing and cleansing**
• Take short, lukewarm showers or baths (no hot water).  
• Add a small amount of gentle, fragrance‑free cleanser or an oatmeal bath product to help soothe the skin.  
• Pat the skin dry gently; do not rub.

**Topical medicines (applied to the skin)**
• **Low‑strength steroid creams** – these reduce redness and itching by calming the immune response in the skin. Use them only as directed, usually for a few days to a week, then stop or switch to a milder option.  
• **Non‑steroid creams (calcineurin inhibitors)** – these also calm inflammation but do not contain steroids; they are useful for sensitive areas like the face or eyelids.  
• **Barrier repair creams** – some products contain special lipids that help rebuild the skin’s natural barrier.

**Itch relief**
• Oral antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine) can help with nighttime itching, making it easier to sleep.  
• Cool compresses or a cool, damp cloth applied to the itchy area can provide quick relief.

**Wet‑wrap therapy**
• After applying moisturizer and any prescribed cream, cover the area with a damp layer of clothing or gauze, then add a dry layer on top. This helps the skin absorb the medication and stay hydrated. It is usually done for a few hours or overnight under a doctor’s guidance.

**Phototherapy (light treatment)**
• In moderate to severe cases that do not improve with creams, a doctor may recommend controlled exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light. This can calm the immune response in the skin.

**Systemic medications (taken by mouth or injection)**
• For severe eczema that does not respond to other treatments, doctors may prescribe stronger medicines such as oral steroids, methotrexate, or newer drugs that target specific immune pathways (called biologics, e.g., dupilumab). These are used only when needed and under close medical supervision.

**Avoiding triggers**
• Identify and stay away from things that worsen the rash, such as certain soaps, detergents, wool clothing, pet dander, or specific foods.  
• Keep nails short to reduce skin damage from scratching.  
• Use a humidifier in dry indoor environments to add moisture to the air.

**Regular follow‑up**
• Work with a dermatologist or primary‑care doctor to adjust treatment as the eczema improves or changes.  
• Keep a simple diary of flare‑ups, products used, and possible triggers; this helps the doctor fine‑tune the plan.

By combining daily skin care, appropriate medicines, and trigger avoidance, most people can keep eczema under control and reduce the uncomfortable itching and redness. If symptoms persist or worsen, it’s important to see a healthcare professional for a personalized plan.

Hypothyroidism means the thyroid gland is not making enough thyroid hormone. The goal of treatment is to replace the missing hormone so the body can work normally.

**Main treatment**

• **Synthetic thyroid hormone (levothyroxine)** – This is a man‑made version of the hormone thyroxine (T4) that the thyroid normally makes. It is taken as a pill once a day, usually in the morning on an empty stomach. The dose is started low and then slowly increased until blood tests show the right hormone level.

**How the dose is set**

• Your doctor will check a blood test called TSH (thyroid‑stimulating hormone).  
• If TSH is high, the dose is raised a little; if it is low, the dose is lowered.  
• Adjustments are usually made every 4‑6 weeks until the level stays in the normal range.

**Things to remember when taking the medicine**

• Take it with a full glass of water and wait at least 30‑60 minutes before eating or drinking anything other than water.  
• Certain foods and supplements (like soy, high‑fiber meals, calcium or iron tablets) can make the medicine less effective, so keep a consistent routine.  
• If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it’s almost time for the next one; then just skip the missed dose.

**Other possible treatments**

• In rare cases where the body cannot convert T4 to the active form T3, a doctor may add a small amount of synthetic T3 (liothyronine).  
• If the thyroid is still present but underactive, some people may have surgery or radioactive iodine treatment, but these are usually for overactive thyroid, not for hypothyroidism.

**Lifestyle and follow‑up**

• Regular check‑ups every 6‑12 months (or more often when the dose is being changed) to keep the hormone level stable.  
• A balanced diet with enough iodine (found in dairy, seafood, and iodized salt) supports thyroid health, but most people get enough from food.  
• Exercise, adequate sleep, and stress management help you feel better while the hormone level is being corrected.

In short, most people with hypothyroidism feel well by taking a daily levothyroxine pill, adjusting the dose as needed, and keeping up with routine blood tests. If you have any concerns or side effects, talk to your healthcare provider.

The flu (influenza) is a contagious virus that spreads mainly through tiny droplets when a sick person coughs, sneezes, or talks. It can also spread when you touch a surface with the virus and then touch your mouth, nose, or eyes. Below are the most effective ways to lower your chances of getting the flu.

• **Get the flu vaccine each year** – The shot trains your immune system (the body’s defense network) to recognize and fight the flu virus. Even if the vaccine isn’t a perfect match, it still reduces the severity of illness.

• **Wash your hands often** – Use soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially after being in public places, before eating, or after blowing your nose. If soap isn’t available, an alcohol‑based hand sanitizer works well.

• **Avoid close contact with sick people** – Keep a distance of about an arm’s length from anyone who is coughing or sneezing. If you’re sick, stay home to protect others.

• **Cover your mouth and nose** – Use a tissue or the inside of your elbow when you cough or sneeze. Throw used tissues away right away and wash your hands afterward.

• **Clean and disinfect high‑touch surfaces** – Wipe down doorknobs, light switches, phones, and keyboards regularly with a disinfectant wipe or spray.

• **Practice good overall health habits** – 
   - Eat a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains.
   - Get enough sleep (7‑9 hours for most adults) to keep your immune system strong.
   - Stay physically active; regular exercise helps your body fight infections.
   - Manage stress, because chronic stress can weaken immunity.

• **Consider antiviral medication if you’re at high risk** – People with certain medical conditions (like asthma, heart disease, or a weakened immune system) may be prescribed antiviral pills or shots after exposure to reduce the chance of getting sick. This should be discussed with a healthcare provider.

By combining vaccination with these everyday habits, you create multiple layers of protection that make it much harder for the flu virus to take hold. Even if you do catch the flu, these steps often lead to a milder illness and a quicker recovery.

Preventing type 2 diabetes mainly means keeping your blood sugar and weight in a healthy range. The good news is that most of the steps you can take are simple lifestyle habits that also improve overall health.

• Maintain a healthy weight  
  • Even a modest loss of 5‑10 % of body weight can lower your risk.  
  • Focus on steady, realistic changes rather than crash diets.

• Eat a balanced, fiber‑rich diet  
  • Choose whole grains, beans, fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds.  
  • Limit sugary drinks, sweets, and refined carbs (like white bread and pastries).  
  • Include a source of protein (lean meat, fish, tofu, legumes) at each meal to help control hunger.

• Control portion sizes  
  • Use smaller plates or measure servings to avoid overeating.  
  • Pay attention to hunger cues and stop eating when you feel satisfied, not stuffed.

• Stay physically active  
  • Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week (for example, brisk walking, cycling, swimming).  
  • Break it into 30‑minute sessions on most days, or shorter bouts that add up.  
  • Add strength‑training exercises (like lifting light weights or using resistance bands) twice a week to build muscle, which helps the body use sugar better.

• Limit sedentary time  
  • If you work at a desk, stand up and move for a few minutes every hour.  
  • Replace some TV or screen time with light activity, such as a short walk.

• Avoid smoking and limit alcohol  
  • Smoking raises insulin resistance, making blood sugar harder to control.  
  • If you drink alcohol, keep it moderate (up to one drink per day for women, up to two for men) and avoid sugary mixers.

• Get enough sleep  
  • Aim for 7‑9 hours of quality sleep each night.  
  • Poor sleep can affect hormones that control appetite and blood sugar.

• Manage stress  
  • Chronic stress can raise blood‑sugar levels.  
  • Try relaxation techniques such as deep breathing, meditation, yoga, or hobbies you enjoy.

• Regular health check‑ups  
  • If you have risk factors (family history, overweight, high blood pressure, or a history of gestational diabetes), ask your doctor to monitor your blood sugar periodically.  
  • Early detection allows for timely lifestyle adjustments.

By combining these habits—healthy eating, regular movement, weight control, and good sleep—you can significantly lower the chance of developing type 2 diabetes. Small, consistent changes are more sustainable than drastic, short‑term fixes.

Kidney stones are hard, crystal‑like deposits that can form in the kidneys and cause pain when they move.  Most of the time they can be prevented by simple changes in what you drink, eat, and how you live.

**Stay well hydrated**  
• Aim for about 2 to 3 liters (about 8‑12 cups) of fluid a day, unless your doctor tells you otherwise.  
• Water is the best choice; it dilutes the substances in urine that can turn into stones.  
• If you find plain water boring, you can add a splash of citrus juice (lemon or orange) – the citric acid can help keep stones from forming.

**Watch your diet**  

*Calcium*  
• Get enough calcium from foods like milk, yogurt, cheese, leafy greens, and fortified plant milks.  
• Calcium binds to oxalate (a stone‑forming substance) in the gut, so it actually helps prevent stones.  
• Avoid taking large calcium supplements without a doctor’s advice, because too much calcium from pills can increase risk.

*Oxalate*  
• Oxalate is a natural compound found in many foods; when it combines with calcium in the urine, stones can form.  
• Limit very high‑oxalate foods if you have a history of oxalate stones: spinach, rhubarb, beets, nuts, chocolate, and tea.  
• Pair oxalate‑rich foods with calcium‑rich foods at the same meal; the calcium will bind the oxalate in the gut and keep it out of the urine.

*Salt (sodium)*  
• Too much salt makes the kidneys excrete more calcium in the urine, which can lead to stones.  
• Keep daily sodium under about 2,300 mg (roughly one teaspoon of table salt).  
• Choose fresh foods over processed ones, and read labels for hidden salt.

*Animal protein*  
• High amounts of meat, fish, and poultry increase the amount of uric acid and reduce citrate (a natural stone inhibitor) in urine.  
• Aim for moderate portions (about 6‑8 ounces a day) and include plant‑based protein sources like beans, lentils, and tofu.

**Maintain a healthy weight**  
• Being overweight can change the chemistry of urine and raise stone risk.  
• Regular physical activity and a balanced diet help keep weight in a healthy range.

**Limit sugary drinks**  
• Soda, especially those with high fructose corn syrup, can raise stone risk.  
• Choose water, herbal tea, or diluted fruit juice instead.

**Consider citrate supplements**  
• If you have a history of certain stones, a doctor may suggest potassium citrate tablets. Citrate is a natural substance that helps keep stone‑forming minerals dissolved.

**Check medications**  
• Some medicines (like certain diuretics, antacids containing calcium, or drugs for seizures) can raise stone risk.  
• Talk to your doctor about any long‑term meds you take and whether alternatives are possible.

**Regular medical follow‑up**  
• If you’ve had stones before, your doctor may test your urine and blood to see which substances are high.  
• Targeted advice (for example, extra calcium, less protein, or specific medications) can be given based on those results.

**Quick checklist for daily stone prevention**

• Drink enough water – aim for clear or light‑yellow urine.  
• Include a serving of calcium‑rich food at each meal.  
• Limit high‑oxalate foods, or pair them with calcium.  
• Keep salt intake low.  
• Eat moderate amounts of animal protein.  
• Stay active and maintain a healthy weight.  
• Choose water over sugary drinks.  

By following these habits, most people can greatly lower their chance of developing kidney stones. If you’ve already had a stone, or if you have a medical condition that affects your kidneys, it’s a good idea to discuss a personalized plan with your healthcare provider.

Urinary tract infections (UTIs) happen when bacteria get into the bladder or urethra (the tube that carries urine out of the body). Keeping the urinary system clean and helping it flush out bacteria can lower the chance of getting an infection.

**Everyday steps to prevent UTIs**

• **Drink plenty of fluids** – Aim for about 6‑8 glasses of water a day. More fluid means you urinate more often, which helps wash bacteria out of the bladder.

• **Empty your bladder regularly** – Don’t hold urine for long periods. Go when you feel the urge, especially after sex.

• **Wipe front to back** – After using the toilet, wipe from the front (genitals) toward the back (anus). This prevents bacteria from the bowel area from moving toward the urethra.

• **Urinate after sexual activity** – Going to the bathroom soon after sex helps flush any bacteria that may have been pushed toward the urethra.

• **Choose breathable underwear** – Cotton underwear and loose‑fitting clothes keep the area dry. Moisture encourages bacterial growth.

• **Avoid irritating products** – Stay away from scented soaps, bubble baths, douches, and feminine hygiene sprays that can irritate the urethra and make it easier for bacteria to stick.

• **Stay hydrated during illness** – If you have a fever or are vomiting, keep drinking fluids so your urine stays dilute and the bladder keeps emptying.

• **Consider cranberry products** – Some studies suggest unsweetened cranberry juice or capsules may make it harder for bacteria to attach to the bladder wall, but they are not a guarantee. Choose products without added sugar.

• **Maintain good bowel habits** – Constipation can press on the bladder and urethra, making it harder to empty fully. Eat fiber‑rich foods and stay hydrated to keep stools soft.

• **Talk to your doctor about preventive antibiotics** – If you get UTIs frequently (more than three a year), a doctor may prescribe a low‑dose antibiotic taken regularly or after sex to keep infections from happening.

**When to seek medical help**

If you notice symptoms such as a burning feeling when you pee, frequent urges to urinate, cloudy or strong‑smelling urine, or pain in the lower belly, see a healthcare provider. Early treatment can prevent the infection from spreading to the kidneys.

By following these simple habits, you can greatly reduce the risk of a urinary tract infection.

Hepatitis B is a virus that can damage the liver. The good news is that there are several ways to keep it from spreading.

• Get the hepatitis B vaccine.  
   The vaccine is given as a series of shots and creates protection that lasts for many years. It is safe for babies, children, and adults.

• Practice safe sex.  
   Use a condom every time you have vaginal, anal, or oral sex. Condoms help stop the virus from moving from one partner to another.

• Don’t share needles or other drug‑using equipment.  
   If you use drugs that need a needle, always use a new, clean one. Sharing needles is a common way the virus spreads.

• Be careful with personal items that might have blood on them.  
   Do not share razors, toothbrushes, or nail clippers, because tiny amounts of blood can carry the virus.

• Make sure blood and medical products are screened.  
   In hospitals and clinics, blood, organ donations, and medical equipment are tested or sterilized to remove the virus.

• Prevent mother‑to‑baby transmission.  
   Babies born to mothers with hepatitis B should receive the first vaccine dose (the “birth dose”) within 24 hours of birth, followed by the regular vaccine series. In some cases, the mother may also take antiviral medicine during pregnancy to lower the risk.

• Practice good hygiene in health‑care settings.  
   Health workers wear gloves and follow strict cleaning rules to avoid accidental exposure to blood.

By combining vaccination with these everyday safety steps, the chance of getting hepatitis B can be reduced dramatically.

Skin cancer is most often caused by damage from ultraviolet (UV) light, which comes from the sun and from tanning beds. Reducing that damage is the best way to lower your risk. Here are simple steps you can take every day:

• **Stay in the shade** when the sun is strongest, usually between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. If you can, sit under a tree, an umbrella, or a building instead of staying in direct sunlight.

• **Cover up** with clothing that blocks UV light. Long‑sleeved shirts, long pants, wide‑brimmed hats, and sunglasses protect skin and eyes. Look for fabrics that say “UPF” (ultraviolet protection factor) for extra protection.

• **Use sunscreen** on any exposed skin. Choose a broad‑spectrum sunscreen (protects against both UVA and UVB rays) with an SPF of at least 30. Apply it generously 15 minutes before going outside, and reapply every two hours, or sooner if you’re swimming or sweating.

• **Avoid tanning beds**. The artificial UV light in those beds can be even more intense than midday sun and greatly increases skin‑cancer risk.

• **Check your skin regularly**. Look for new spots or changes in existing moles. The ABCDE rule can help you spot warning signs:
  - **A**symmetry – one half of the spot doesn’t match the other.
  - **B**order – edges are irregular, ragged, or blurred.
  - **C**olor – multiple shades or a color that’s different from your normal skin tone.
  - **D**iameter – larger than about 6 mm (roughly the size of a pencil eraser).
  - **E**volving – any change in size, shape, color, or feeling.

• **See a doctor** if you notice anything suspicious. A dermatologist (skin doctor) can examine the spot and, if needed, take a small sample (biopsy) to check for cancer cells.

• **Maintain a healthy lifestyle**. While diet and exercise don’t directly prevent skin cancer, staying healthy supports your immune system, which helps your body repair skin damage.

By making shade, clothing, sunscreen, and regular skin checks part of your routine, you can greatly lower the chance of developing skin cancer.

Hypertension, often called high blood pressure, is a condition where the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries is consistently too high.  

When the heart pumps, it creates pressure to move blood through the circulatory system. If that pressure stays above normal levels for a long time, the arteries have to work harder, which can damage them and lead to other health problems.

**Key points about hypertension**

• Normal blood pressure is usually around 120/80 mm Hg (the numbers are measured in millimeters of mercury).  
• Hypertension is generally defined as a reading of 130/80 mm Hg or higher.  
• It often has no obvious symptoms, which is why it’s called the “silent killer.”  
• Over time, high pressure can strain the heart, damage blood vessels, and increase the risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, and vision problems.  

**What causes it?**  
• Genetics – it can run in families.  
• Lifestyle factors – too much salt, lack of exercise, being overweight, smoking, and excessive alcohol use.  
• Other health conditions – such as kidney disease, hormonal disorders, or certain medications.  

**How is it managed?**  
• Lifestyle changes – eating a balanced diet low in salt, staying active, maintaining a healthy weight, limiting alcohol, and quitting smoking.  
• Medications – doctors may prescribe pills that help relax blood vessels, reduce fluid volume, or lower heart rate.  

Because hypertension usually doesn’t cause noticeable signs, regular check‑ups and blood‑pressure measurements are important to catch it early and keep it under control.

Irritable bowel syndrome, often called IBS, is a common condition that affects the way the large intestine (the part of the gut that stores waste) works. It does not cause damage to the intestine, but it can cause uncomfortable symptoms that come and go.

**What happens in IBS?**  
The muscles in the wall of the colon may contract too strongly or too weakly. This irregular movement can make food move through the gut too quickly or too slowly, leading to the symptoms people notice.

**Typical symptoms**

• Abdominal pain or cramping that often improves after a bowel movement  
• Bloating or a feeling of fullness in the belly  
• Changes in stool pattern, such as:
   – Diarrhea (loose, watery stools)  
   – Constipation (hard, difficult‑to‑pass stools)  
   – Sometimes alternating between diarrhea and constipation  

**What can trigger symptoms?**  
Many people find that certain foods, stress, hormonal changes, or a stomach infection can make IBS flare up. Common triggers include:

• Fatty or fried foods  
• Spicy foods  
• Caffeine or alcohol  
• Large meals or eating quickly  
• Stressful situations or anxiety  

**How is IBS diagnosed?**  
There is no single test for IBS. Doctors usually:

1. Take a detailed medical history and ask about symptoms.  
2. Perform a physical exam.  
3. Use criteria that look at the pattern of pain and bowel changes (for example, the Rome criteria).  
4. Order tests only if they need to rule out other conditions such as infections, inflammatory bowel disease, or celiac disease.

**Managing IBS**

• Diet changes  
   – Try a low‑FODMAP diet (reduces certain fermentable carbs that can cause gas).  
   – Increase fiber gradually if constipation is a problem.  
   – Keep a food diary to spot personal triggers.  

• Stress reduction  
   – Relaxation techniques like deep breathing, meditation, or yoga.  
   – Regular exercise, which can help both digestion and mood.  

• Medications (prescribed by a doctor)  
   – Fiber supplements or laxatives for constipation.  
   – Anti‑diarrheal medicines for frequent loose stools.  
   – Antispasmodic drugs to lessen cramping.  
   – Sometimes low‑dose antidepressants are used to help with pain and stress.  

**When to see a doctor**  
If you notice any of the following, it’s important to get medical advice:

• Blood in the stool  
• Unexplained weight loss  
• Severe or worsening pain  
• Symptoms that start after age 50  

Overall, IBS is a functional disorder, meaning the gut works differently but isn’t damaged. With lifestyle adjustments, stress management, and, when needed, medication, most people can keep symptoms under control and lead normal lives.

Kidney stones form when substances that are normally dissolved in urine become too concentrated and start to stick together. Several factors can make this happen:

• **Not drinking enough fluids** – When you’re dehydrated, urine is more concentrated, giving crystals a better chance to grow.

• **Dietary habits** – Eating a lot of foods high in salt, animal protein (like meat, eggs, and fish), or oxalate (found in spinach, nuts, chocolate, and tea) can increase the amount of stone‑forming chemicals in the urine.

• **Certain medical conditions** – Some illnesses raise the level of stone‑forming substances, such as:
  – High blood calcium (hypercalcemia) from conditions like hyperparathyroidism.
  – Gout, which raises uric acid.
  – Infections of the urinary tract that produce certain chemicals.

• **Family history and genetics** – If close relatives have had stones, you may be more likely to develop them.

• **Medications** – Some drugs, like certain diuretics, calcium‑based antacids, or medications used for HIV, can increase stone risk.

• **Obesity and metabolic syndrome** – Excess weight can change the balance of chemicals in urine, making stones more likely.

When these factors cause the urine to become supersaturated with minerals such as calcium, oxalate, uric acid, or cystine, tiny crystals form. Over time they can grow into a stone that may stay in the kidney or travel down the urinary tract, causing pain and possible blockage. Drinking plenty of water, eating a balanced diet, and managing underlying health issues are the main ways to lower the risk.

Polycystic ovary syndrome, often called PCOS, is a common health condition that affects people who have ovaries. It involves a mix of hormonal changes and how the ovaries work.

**What happens in PCOS**

• The ovaries may have many small, immature follicles (tiny fluid‑filled sacs) that look like cysts on an ultrasound.  
• Hormone levels are out of balance, especially higher amounts of androgens (male‑type hormones) and sometimes too much insulin.  
• Because of the hormone shift, the ovaries may not release an egg each month, leading to irregular periods or missed periods.

**Common signs and symptoms**

• Irregular or absent menstrual periods  
• Extra hair growth on the face, chest, or back (called hirsutism)  
• Acne or oily skin, especially in adult years  
• Thinning hair on the scalp (similar to male‑pattern baldness)  
• Weight gain or difficulty losing weight, often around the belly  
• Dark patches of skin, especially on the neck or under the arms (called acanthosis nigricans)  
• Trouble getting pregnant because ovulation is irregular

**Why it occurs**

The exact cause isn’t known, but several factors can play a role:

• Genetics – it often runs in families.  
• Insulin resistance – the body’s cells don’t respond well to insulin, so the pancreas makes more, which can raise androgen levels.  
• Low‑grade inflammation – a mild, ongoing inflammation that can affect hormone production.

**How doctors diagnose it**

Doctors usually look for at least two of the following three features:

1. Irregular or absent periods.  
2. Signs of excess androgens (like hirsutism or acne).  
3. Polycystic ovaries seen on an ultrasound.

They may also run blood tests to check hormone levels and rule out other conditions.

**Treatment options**

Treatment is tailored to the person’s main concerns, such as regulating periods, reducing acne, or helping with fertility.

• Lifestyle changes – a balanced diet, regular exercise, and modest weight loss can improve insulin resistance and hormone balance.  
• Birth‑control pills – help regulate periods and lower androgen levels, which can improve acne and hair growth.  
• Anti‑androgen medications – such as spironolactone, can reduce excess hair growth and acne.  
• Metformin – a medication that improves insulin sensitivity, sometimes used when insulin resistance is a big issue.  
• Fertility medicines – like clomiphene or letrozole, can stimulate ovulation when pregnancy is desired.  
• Cosmetic treatments – laser hair removal or electrolysis for unwanted hair, and dermatology options for acne.

**Living with PCOS**

• Regular check‑ups help monitor symptoms and adjust treatment.  
• Keeping a healthy weight, even a small loss of 5‑10 % of body weight, often makes a big difference in symptoms.  
• Managing stress, getting enough sleep, and staying active support overall hormone balance.  

If you think you might have PCOS, talk to a healthcare provider. They can evaluate your symptoms, run the necessary tests, and create a plan that fits your needs.

Anemia is a condition where the blood does not have enough healthy red blood cells or enough hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen. When there aren’t enough red blood cells, the body’s tissues don’t get the oxygen they need, which can cause tiredness, shortness of breath, and a pale appearance.

**Main reasons anemia can develop**

• **Blood loss** – Losing blood reduces the number of red cells. This can happen from:
  – Heavy menstrual periods
  – Surgery or injury that causes bleeding
  – Gastrointestinal bleeding from ulcers, hemorrhoids, or colon cancer

• **Not enough red‑cell production** – The bone marrow (the spongy tissue inside bones that makes blood cells) may not make enough red cells because of:
  – Iron deficiency (iron is a mineral needed to build hemoglobin)
  – Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency (these vitamins help the body form new red cells)
  – Chronic kidney disease (the kidneys make a hormone that tells the marrow to produce red cells)
  – Certain medicines or chemotherapy that suppress the marrow

• **Red‑cell destruction (hemolysis)** – Sometimes red cells break down faster than they can be replaced. Causes include:
  – Autoimmune diseases where the body attacks its own cells
  – Infections such as malaria
  – Inherited conditions like sickle‑cell disease or thalassemia (genes that affect the shape or production of hemoglobin)

• **Chronic diseases** – Long‑standing illnesses such as cancer, rheumatoid arthritis, or inflammatory bowel disease can interfere with red‑cell production, leading to what doctors call “anemia of chronic disease.”

• **Inherited (genetic) disorders** – Some people are born with genes that affect how hemoglobin is made or how red cells function, resulting in lifelong anemia.

In many cases, more than one factor can contribute. Identifying the specific cause helps doctors choose the right treatment, whether it’s dietary changes, supplements, medication, or other therapies.

Yes. Smoking is the single biggest cause of lung cancer.

Why smoking raises the risk  

• Tobacco smoke contains thousands of chemicals, many of which are known to damage DNA. DNA is the instruction manual inside each cell; when it is damaged, cells can start to grow out of control, which is what cancer is.  

• The more cigarettes a person smokes and the longer they have smoked, the higher the risk. Even a few cigarettes a day for many years can increase the chance of developing lung cancer.  

• People who quit smoking lower their risk over time. After about 10 years without smoking, the risk drops to roughly half of that of a current smoker, and after 15–20 years it approaches the level of someone who never smoked.

How big is the effect  

• About 85 % of all lung‑cancer cases in the United States are linked to smoking.  

• A lifelong smoker is roughly 20 times more likely to get lung cancer than a person who never smoked.  

• Even occasional or “light” smokers have a noticeably higher risk than non‑smokers.

What can be done  

• Stopping smoking at any age reduces the chance of lung cancer and improves overall health.  

• Support options include counseling, nicotine‑replacement products (like patches or gum), and prescription medicines that help reduce cravings.  

• Avoiding second‑hand smoke—breathing in other people’s tobacco smoke—also lowers risk.

In short, smoking dramatically increases the chance of lung cancer, but quitting can significantly cut that risk.

Aspirin is commonly used after a heart attack to help prevent another one. This use is called “secondary prevention” because the goal is to stop a second event in someone who already has heart disease.

Why aspirin helps  
• Aspirin blocks a substance called thromboxane, which makes platelets (tiny blood‑cell fragments) stick together and form clots.  
• After a heart attack, the arteries are already narrowed or damaged, so clots are more likely to form and block blood flow again. By keeping platelets from clumping, aspirin reduces the chance of a new blockage.

What the research shows  
• Large studies have found that people who take a low‑dose aspirin (usually 75–100 mg daily) after a heart attack have about a 20 % lower risk of another heart attack or death from heart disease.  
• The benefit is seen in most patients, especially those who have had a heart attack, a stent placed, or bypass surgery.

Who should take it  
• Most adults who have survived a heart attack are advised to take a daily low‑dose aspirin unless they have a strong reason not to.  
• Situations where aspirin may be avoided or used with caution include:  
  • Active bleeding or a history of serious stomach ulcers  
  • Certain blood‑clotting disorders  
  • Allergy to aspirin or other non‑steroidal anti‑inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)  
  • Some people on other blood‑thinning medications where the combined bleeding risk is high

Possible side effects  
• The main risk is bleeding, especially in the stomach or intestines, and sometimes easy bruising.  
• Taking aspirin with food, using the lowest effective dose, and having a doctor monitor for signs of bleeding can lower this risk.

What to do next  
• If you have already had a heart attack, talk with your doctor about starting or continuing low‑dose aspirin.  
• Your doctor will consider your overall health, other medicines, and any bleeding risk before recommending it.  
• Never start or stop aspirin on your own; the dose and need can differ from person to person.

In short, for most people who have had a heart attack, taking a low‑dose aspirin daily does reduce the chance of another heart attack, but the decision should be made together with a healthcare professional who can weigh the benefits against the bleeding risk.

Yes. Being overweight or obese makes it more likely that a person will develop knee osteoarthritis, and it can also make the condition worse.

Why extra weight matters  

• The knee joint carries the weight of the whole upper body. When a person carries extra pounds, the joint has to bear more pressure every time they stand, walk, or climb stairs.  
• This added pressure can wear down the smooth cartilage that cushions the ends of the bones. Over time the cartilage becomes thinner and rough, which is the hallmark of osteoarthritis.  
• Fat tissue releases chemicals called inflammatory cytokines. These substances can cause low‑grade inflammation in the joint, further damaging cartilage and the surrounding structures.

How strong is the link?  

• Studies show that for each additional 5 kg (about 11 lb) of body weight, the risk of knee osteoarthritis goes up by roughly 10 percent.  
• People with a body‑mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m² or higher (the usual definition of obesity) have about twice the risk of developing knee osteoarthritis compared with people of normal weight.  
• The risk is even higher for women, who tend to develop knee osteoarthritis at lower BMI levels than men.

What does this mean for someone who is already overweight?  

• Carrying extra weight not only raises the chance of getting knee osteoarthritis, it can also make symptoms—pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility—worse.  
• Losing weight can reduce the load on the knee. Even a modest loss of 5–10 % of body weight can lower knee‑joint pressure by about 30–40 percent, which often leads to less pain and improved function.  

What can help  

• A balanced diet that creates a gradual calorie deficit.  
• Regular low‑impact exercise such as walking, swimming, or cycling, which strengthens the muscles around the knee without putting too much stress on the joint.  
• Physical‑therapy programs that teach proper movement patterns and strengthen the quadriceps and hip muscles, helping the knee bear weight more efficiently.  

In short, obesity is a clear and modifiable risk factor for knee osteoarthritis. Reducing body weight can lower the chance of developing the disease and can also ease symptoms if osteoarthritis is already present.

Yes. Infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori (often called H. pylori) is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease.

**Why the link exists**

- H. pylori lives in the lining of the stomach and the upper part of the small intestine.  
- It produces substances that damage the protective mucus layer, allowing stomach acid to irritate the underlying tissue.  
- The irritation and inflammation can create a sore, or ulcer, in the stomach lining (gastric ulcer) or in the first part of the small intestine (duodenal ulcer).  

**How common is the connection?**

- About 70‑90 % of people with duodenal ulcers and roughly 50‑70 % of those with gastric ulcers have an active H. pylori infection.  
- In populations where the bacterium is common, most peptic ulcers are linked to it; in places where the infection is rare, other causes (such as long‑term use of non‑steroidal anti‑inflammatory drugs, NSAIDs) become more important.

**What this means for patients**

- Testing for H. pylori (breath test, stool test, blood test, or endoscopic biopsy) is recommended when an ulcer is diagnosed.  
- If the infection is present, a short course of antibiotics together with medicines that reduce stomach acid usually heals the ulcer and lowers the chance it will come back.  
- Even if the ulcer is caused by NSAIDs, checking for H. pylori is still useful because treating the infection can help protect the stomach.

**Bottom line**

Helicobacter pylori infection is strongly associated with peptic ulcer disease and is considered one of the main causes of these ulcers. Detecting and treating the infection is a key part of managing and preventing ulcer problems.

Yes. The human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine has been shown to lower the number of women who develop cervical precancer.

• What cervical precancer is  
  Cervical precancer refers to abnormal cells on the cervix that are not yet cancer but could become cancer if they are not treated. Doctors usually call these changes CIN 2 or CIN 3 (CIN = cervical intra‑epithelial neoplasia, a term for early cell changes).

• How the vaccine works  
  The vaccine protects against the HPV types that cause most cervical precancers—especially HPV 16 and HPV 18, which together are responsible for about 70 % of cases. By preventing infection with these high‑risk viruses, the vaccine stops the chain that can lead to abnormal cells.

• Evidence from studies  
  Large studies in countries that introduced the vaccine (such as Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States) have found:  
  - A 50 %‑80 % drop in the rates of CIN 2/3 lesions among vaccinated girls and young women.  
  - In populations where most girls received the vaccine before becoming sexually active, the overall number of cervical precancers fell dramatically within a few years.  
  - The reduction is greatest when the vaccine is given at ages 9‑14, before any exposure to HPV.

• What this means for you  
  If you receive the vaccine before you are exposed to HPV, you are much less likely to develop the early cell changes that can turn into cervical cancer later. The vaccine does not treat existing infections, so it works best when given early.

• Screening is still important  
  Even vaccinated women should continue regular cervical screening (Pap tests or HPV tests) because the vaccine does not protect against every cancer‑causing HPV type, and some women may have been exposed before vaccination.

In short, the HPV vaccine significantly reduces the incidence of cervical precancer, especially when given to adolescents before they become sexually active. Regular screening remains a key part of protecting cervical health.

Cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) is a type of talk therapy that helps people change unhelpful thoughts and habits. When it is focused on sleep, it is called CBT‑I (cognitive‑behavioral therapy for insomnia).

**What the research says**

• Many well‑controlled studies have found that CBT‑I reduces the time it takes to fall asleep, shortens nighttime awakenings, and increases total sleep time.
